name: Imperial Purple
lede: Imperial purple was the shellfish dye of Rome and Byzantium, so costly that emperors fenced it with law; the muted blue-violet that carries its name on screen comes from a nineteenth-century mineralogist's color chart, not from the dye.

sections.title: Two imperial purples
sections.body:
The swatch here, #584C77, is a muted blue-violet [7]. The nearest ISCC-NBS block is "grayish violet", 3.1 units away, and the name Imperial Purple is listed in a neighboring block of that 1955 dictionary [7].

The dye the name points to was something else. Greenfield says the dye was in fact a range of colors, from deep scarlet and crimson to [[gem:amethyst|amethyst]] and violet tones [1]. Gage adds that redness and lustre seem to have been the most prized qualities of ancient and medieval purple, more than any one hue [4]. The name belonged to a rank first and a color second.

The Latin word *purpura* has a doubtful etymology in the books [3]. Isidore of Seville suggested it came from words meaning "purity of light", and Finlay thinks that is probably not true [3].

sections.title: The snail and the vat
sections.body:
The dye came from sea snails of the Muricidae and Thaisidae families [2]. It does not exist ready-made in the animal: it forms from precursor chemicals held in a gland, which is one reason ancient accounts of the process are so hard to reconstruct [2]. The Pigment Compendium finds evidence of a dye industry at Sarepta, in today's Lebanon, as early as the thirteenth century BC [2].

The chemistry came late. The main component, 6,6'-dibromoindigotin, was identified only in the first half of the twentieth century, and two further components in 1992 [2]. The name already hints at the relation: in 1908 Paul Friedlaender showed that imperial purple is chemically very close to indigo [3].

That kinship explains why a snail dye could come out blue. Finlay reports that in the 1980s the chemist Otto Elsner found that dyeing done on a sunny day came out blue and on a cloudy day purple [3]. Long before, in 1685, the naturalist William Cole watched a shellfish dye left in the sun pass from green through blue to a purplish red and finally a very deep purple red [10]. The color was never one color, and the vat and the weather decided the result.

sections.title: Price and law
sections.body:
Dyers had to crush thousands of snails to dye a single garment [1]. In the fourth century, in Diocletian's reign, the finest imperial purple cloth was priced at 50,000 denarii a pound and cheaper grades at 16,000, while a stoneworker made 50 denarii a day [1]. By that arithmetic a pound of the best cloth equalled a thousand days of a stoneworker's pay.

The law followed the price. For holidays and feasts the cloth was open only to senators and other leading men, and under Caligula, Nero and the fourth-century emperors its use was restricted to the imperial family [1]. Greenfield notes that the evidence suggests many elite Romans wore some shades of it anyway, and Pliny recorded a double-dyed variety used to cover dining couches [1].

Fashion moved inside the privilege. In the early first century wealthy Romans preferred purples that leaned toward red, and about fifty years later the most desirable shade was a mixture of scarlet and purple-black dyes [1]. Finlay's notes add that Pliny described the blackness as made with two shellfish, the small buccinum giving a crimson-like sheen to the larger purpura, and that people of Pliny's own day seemed to favor a lighter shade [10].

sections.title: Hue, shine and doubt
sections.body:
Because the name covered a range, the surviving images disagree about the color. Gage reads the Empress Theodora's robe in the Ravenna mosaic as announcing the true imperial purple by its shine rather than its hue [4]. In a Byzantine scene of Mary receiving the skein of wool, an inscription calls the cloth *porphyrion*, yet the painted color is a clear vermilion red [4].

The filmmaker and painter Derek Jarman asks the same question from the other side: since the Greeks had no word for a true blue, was imperial purple in fact red [5]? It is a question, not a finding, but it matches what the other books say.

The long search for the blue thread of Jewish ritual, *tekhelet*, ran into the same problem [3]. The Hebrew word can suggest both violet and blue, scholars were convinced the historical color leaned toward blue, and whatever they made from the shellfish usually came out purple [3]. Finlay says the experimenter John Edmonds, who had worked on woad, was sent a vial of pigment and some wool to test whether the dye, like indigo, needs oxygen removed from the vat before it will dye [3].

sections.title: The end of the dye
sections.body:
When the dye stopped is something the books do not agree on. Greenfield says Constantinople was the sole source of the old Roman dye by 1295, when the pope decreed that cardinals would wear "red" robes that were actually a reddish imperial purple, and that the supply dried up for good when the city fell in 1453 [1]. Finlay says the dyers had disappeared with the fall of Constantinople or even before, and that the last recorded mention of purple dyeing as a going trade may be Benjamin of Tudela's account of Jewish silk and purple makers at Thebes in 1165 [3].

Greenfield adds that the Church then switched to a red European dye made partly with alum, and cardinals dressed in scarlet from then on [1]. The date when cardinals took scarlet is one of the points where the books differ, so treat any single year with care.

Perkin's mauve revived interest in the older purple. Finlay reports that within four years of his discovery Napoleon III sent an archaeological expedition to find out where Tyre was and whether anything of its riches remained [3]. The story of that discovery is told under [[mauve]]; the story of the dye itself is under [[tyrian-purple]] and [[royal-purple]].

sections.title: A naturalist's imperial purple
sections.body:
The modern swatch comes from a different tradition. In 1774 the German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner devised a nomenclature of 54 colors to identify minerals, and in 1814 the Scottish artist Patrick Syme expanded it to 108 terms, then to 110 in 1821 [6]. Maerz and Paul give 1814 as the first record of Imperial Purple, which fits Syme's first edition [7].

In that chart Imperial Purple is number 40, among the purples [6][7]. Its natural examples are the deep parts of the flower of the saffron crocus and the mineral fluorspar, and the recipe calls for azure blue and indigo blue with carmine red, about equal parts of each [6][7]. The modern edition of the chart adds a metallic starling's feathers as an animal example [6]. Syme's own swatches have grown more muted with age, so even this chart color has drifted [6].

Neighbors in the same chart are [[campanula-purple]] and [[pansy-purple]], and our library records [[anthracene-violet]] as almost the same screen color [6][7]. Our library also lists the Japanese traditional name Benikakehana-iro (紅掛花色, "safflower color") against this swatch; the match is by screen color, not by dye [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
As a painted color this dusky violet is rare. In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 16 works [8]. The painting with the most is [[painter:gustav-klimt|Klimt]]'s [[painting:commons-Q5967091|The Maiden]] at 18 per cent of the canvas, and his [[painting:commons-Q140248069|Irrlichter]] follows at 14 per cent [8]. Three of the 50 Klimt paintings in the archive qualify, about 89 times the rate for the archive as a whole [8].

Six of the 1,674 paintings from the 1900s qualify, against six of the 8,345 from the 1800s [8]. Three quarters of the matching areas sit in a painting's shadows [8]. The earliest match with at least five per cent of the canvas is a Filippo Lippi *Coronation of the Virgin* from 1441, 373 years before the name's first record, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph and not evidence of the dye [8]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [8].

In Google Books the phrase *imperial purple* peaks around 1804, at the start of the data's range [9]. By 1860 it is at about 35 per cent of that peak and by 1940 at about 4 per cent [9]. The count covers every sense of the phrase, including the ancient dye, so it reflects classical writing as much as color.

questions.q: Why do the sources describe imperial purple as anything from scarlet to violet?
choices: The name covered a range of shades, and lustre and intensity mattered as much as hue
Every dyer used a different shellfish from a different ocean
The color changed with the age of the cloth, not the vat
Rome had a single recipe but copyists mislabeled it
questions.answer: The name covered a range of shades, and lustre and intensity mattered as much as hue

questions.q: True or false: the modern swatch called Imperial Purple is a faithful copy of the Roman dye.
In 1908 Paul Friedlaender showed that imperial purple is chemically very close to which dye?

openers: Under Diocletian a pound of the best imperial purple cloth cost 50,000 denarii while a stoneworker earned 50 a day.
The same snail dye can dye blue on a sunny day and purple on a cloudy one.
In the Ravenna mosaics, look for the shine of the purple robes, not their hue.
